extracted.intended_audience: public companies' legal, investor-relations, communications, and compliance teams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public companies on using social media for investor disclosures and how to prevent or remediate Regulation FD (Reg FD) violations arising from selective or untimely social-media communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg FD simultaneous public disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a company discloses material, nonpublic information selectively (e.g., to certain investors or via channels not broadly available), Reg FD requires that the same information be disclosed to all investors simultaneously via a press release or a Form 8-K (or other broadly disseminated method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If material information is conveyed through a non-FD-compliant channel, the company must promptly make the information public through an FD-compliant channel; failure to do so can lead to enforcement (example: SEC charged a company and the company paid a $200,000 civil penalty).

rubrics_metrics.name: If using social media as a disclosure channel, notify investors via Form 8-K
rubrics_metrics.description: A company that plans to use social media to disclose material information should first make investors aware of which social media accounts it will use (e.g., by filing a Form 8-K notifying investors of those channels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once investors are informed of social-media channels in a Form 8-K, the company should actually use those channels for consistent communications so that investors who rely on those channels are not disadvantaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing sensitivity around earnings and quiet periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must be especially careful about the timing of social-media posts relative to earnings statements and quiet periods; reiterating prior statements can nonetheless be perceived as conveying new material information depending on timing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before posting (or allowing third parties to post), consider whether the content could be viewed as new material information given the company's reporting calendar (example: a post after quarter close but before 10-Q filing was treated as nonpublic information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deletion is not an adequate cure for selective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a non-intentional selective disclosure is made via social media or other channels, simply deleting the post or communication will generally not cure the Reg FD violation in the SEC's view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should promptly issue a press release or file a Form 8-K to disseminate the same information broadly — ideally the same day as the disclosure or, at most, within 24 hours. The DraftKings example: posts were deleted within 30 minutes, but the company did not promptly disclose broadly and later faced enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous pre-publication review and internal approval controls for social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure controls should include a robust review process for social-media content, ensuring all necessary internal approvals are obtained before posts are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As use of social media and outside PR firms grows, companies must incorporate social-media oversight into disclosure controls to prevent inadvertent selective disclosure; this includes clear sign-offs and checklists for materiality and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company responsibility for third-party/PR firm communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications posted by outside public-relations firms or third parties can create Reg FD liability for the company if the content was reviewed/approved by company staff or otherwise attributable to the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should treat outside-party posts as company communications for compliance purposes and apply the same review/approval and dissemination procedures; do not rely on 'outside party posted it' as a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether reiterations may convey new material information
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a post merely reiterates previously disclosed information (e.g., that prior statements remain accurate as of a later date), companies must evaluate whether that reiteration could be construed as conveying new material information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When restating prior information via social media, consider whether the update (date/context/timing) changes investors' view; if it could, treat it as a material disclosure and disseminate through FD-compliant channels.
